name: The fruit in disguise (culinary vegetable vs botanical fruit)
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: The one rule that decides 'fruit': it grew from the flower and it carries the seeds — no matter how savory it tastes. T1: a tomato is botanically a FRUIT because it grows from the plant's flower and holds the seeds inside, even though the kitchen treats it as a vegetable. T2: 'vegetable' is a KITCHEN word (savory, for main dishes), not a botanical one — so a cucumber, bell pepper, eggplant, zucchini and green bean are all botanical fruits too, because each one carries seeds. T3: a pumpkin (and every winter squash) is a single giant fruit — a hard-rinded berry called a pepo — and the scoop of seeds inside is the proof. T3b: an avocado is a fruit with one big stone-seed and an olive is a one-seeded fruit (a drupe) — 'fruit' does not mean 'sweet'. T4 (food-history): in 1893 the US Supreme Court (Nix v. Hedden) ruled the tomato a VEGETABLE for import-tax purposes, siding with everyday kitchen use over botany because the tariff taxed vegetables but not fruit. T5 (dinner-test payoff): a true berry is a fleshy fruit whose seeds sit INSIDE, grown from one flower's single ovary — so a tomato, grape and even a banana are berries, but a strawberry (seeds on the OUTSIDE, built from many ovaries) is not a true berry at all.
source: Verified: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nix_v._Hedden (1893 ruling, Tariff Act of 1883). Botanical fruit/berry/pepo/drupe and strawberry-is-an-accessory-fruit are settled botany (Grokipedia attempted first, HTTP 403; corroborate at build via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fruit and /Berry_(botany)).
framing_note: Scene-led: 'slice it open and count the seeds' — never 'What is a fruit?'. Both labels are valid in their own domain; do NOT sneer at 'vegetable' — the point is the two words answer different questions (kitchen use vs botany). The Nix v. Hedden rung is food-anchored (the tomato and its tariff are the subject, not the court). Dinner-test payoff = the strawberry-isn't-a-berry rung. Keep the seed-carrying clue OUT of the stem so all four choices stay live.

name: One wild plant, a whole produce aisle (Brassica oleracea)
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: The same single species — Brassica oleracea — was bred into a shelf of totally different vegetables by exaggerating a different plant PART each time. T1: kale and cabbage are the same species of plant — farmers just selected for loose open leaves (kale, collards) or a tight wrapped head of leaves (cabbage). T2: broccoli and cauliflower are that SAME species again, but here the selected part is the flower head — leave broccoli in the garden and its green buds open into yellow flowers. T3 (dinner-test payoff): Brussels sprouts are the same species too — they are the little leaf-buds that grow in a column up a tall stalk, so a stalk of sprouts is a row of miniature cabbages; kohlrabi is the same species bred for a swollen edible STEM. T4 (the concept): this is artificial selection — one scrubby wild coastal cabbage of the Mediterranean, pushed over centuries by farmers choosing bigger leaves, buds, flowers or stems, became half a dozen 'different' vegetables (the same power Darwin pointed to in dog and pigeon breeds). T5: not every cabbagey vegetable is B. oleracea — the turnip, bok choy and napa cabbage are a different species (Brassica rapa), and the rutabaga and the canola-oil plant are another (Brassica napus).
source: Verified: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brassica_oleracea (cultivar groups Acephala/Capitata/Botrytis/Gemmifera/Gongylodes and the emphasized organ each; wild relative Brassica cretica of the E. Mediterranean; B. rapa and B. napus are separate species). Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403).
framing_note: Lead with the surprise ('six vegetables in your fridge are one species') — never 'What is Brassica oleracea?'; the Latin name is context, never the tested answer. Accuracy rail: this is centuries of farmer selection, NOT a modern lab/GMO trick, and the ancestor is a wild Mediterranean cabbage (not 'wild broccoli'). Dinner-test payoff = Brussels-sprouts-are-buds-up-a-stalk. Keep answers food-anchored (a vegetable or its part), not the bare word 'selection'.

name: The potato: a stem that grew underground (tubers)
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: A potato is not a root — it is a swollen underground STEM (a tuber) the plant packs with starch, and that identity explains its eyes, its poison, and its history. T1: a potato is a TUBER — a swollen underground stem, not a root; the 'eyes' are buds, and a chunk with an eye will sprout a whole new plant, which is why potatoes are grown from potatoes, not seeds. T2 (origin): the potato is Andean — domesticated thousands of years ago high in the mountains of Peru and Bolivia near Lake Titicaca, long before it reached Europe. T3 (same-name surprise): a sweet potato is NOT a potato — it is a storage ROOT of a different plant (a morning-glory relative), while the true potato is a stem; same name, different organ, different family. T4 (honest safety): a green or heavily sprouted potato is building up solanine, a natural toxin (the potato is in the nightshade family), so the green tinge under the skin is a warning to cut it away. T5a (food-history): after 1492 the Columbian Exchange carried the potato to Europe, where its huge calories-per-acre helped populations and armies boom. T5b (dinner-test payoff): the Irish Great Famine (1845) hit so hard because the poor lived on one cloned variety (the 'Lumper') with no genetic variety — so when the blight Phytophthora infestans arrived, the whole crop rotted at once (a monoculture catastrophe).
source: Verified: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato (stem tuber not root; eyes are buds; Andes near Lake Titicaca ~7,000-10,000 yrs; Solanaceae/solanine in green potatoes; Columbian Exchange; 1845 Great Famine, Phytophthora infestans, Lumper). Sweet-potato-is-a-root/Convolvulaceae: settled botany. Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403).
framing_note: Scene-first ('dig one up — why does it grow eyes?'), never 'What is a tuber?'. Accuracy rails: potato = Andean (never Irish/European in origin); tuber = STEM not root; sweet potato is a different plant and a root. The famine rung is food-anchored (the blight and the monoculture crop are the subject, not British policy) and is the dinner-test payoff. Keep the solanine rung matter-of-fact, not scary.

name: Grains: the seed that built civilization
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: The world's staple grains are grass SEEDS, and how we mill and treat that one seed decides whether it nourishes or sickens whole peoples. T1: wheat, rice, corn and oats are all grasses, and the grain we eat is the plant's SEED, packed with starch to feed the next generation of grass. T2 (dinner-test payoff): a wheat kernel has three parts — the bran (fibrous coat), the germ (the living embryo) and the endosperm (the big starchy store); white flour is JUST the endosperm, while whole-wheat keeps all three. T3 (origin): corn (maize) is a giant grass bred in Mexico from a scraggly wild grass called teosinte — the cob and its rows of huge seeds are entirely a human creation, not a wild plant. T4 (food-history): milling rice white strips off the bran and germ and, with them, its thiamine (vitamin B1) — peoples living on polished white rice developed beriberi, a nerve-and-heart disease, until the missing vitamin was traced to the discarded bran. T5 (food-history): nixtamalization — soaking corn in an alkali such as lime or wood ash, invented in ancient Mesoamerica — unlocks the grain's niacin; peoples who took up corn WITHOUT this step, in Europe and the US South, suffered pellagra, a niacin-deficiency disease.
source: Verified: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_rice (milling removes bran/germ + thiamine, beriberi), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixtamalization (alkali unlocks niacin, prevents pellagra, Mesoamerican origin). Maize-from-teosinte (Mexico) and wheat caryopsis bran/germ/endosperm are settled (corroborate at build via /Maize and /Wheat). Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403).
framing_note: Lead with the food/scene ('name the three layers inside a grain of wheat'), never a dictionary 'What is a grain?'. Accuracy rails: maize is Mesoamerican (from teosinte), never Old-World; nixtamalization is ancient Mesoamerican. Beriberi and pellagra rungs are food-anchored (the milled grain / the untreated corn is the subject). Dinner-test payoff = the bran/germ/endosperm rung (why white vs whole). Teach the concept — the vitamin's chemistry is context, not the tested answer.

name: Every spice is a plant part in disguise
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: Reach into a spice rack and you are holding a botany lesson — each spice is a different plant ORGAN, and one of them was worth killing for. T1: black pepper (the peppercorn) is a dried FRUIT — a tiny berry — of a tropical climbing vine; green, black and white pepper are the same berry picked and processed differently. T2: cinnamon is BARK — the inner bark of a tree, peeled and dried, which curls up on its own into the familiar quill. T3 (invert-the-wonder): vanilla, the flavor everyone knows, is the cured seed POD (fruit) of a climbing orchid — the only orchid grown for food — and outside its native Mexico it must be pollinated BY HAND, a method figured out in 1841 by Edmond Albius, an enslaved boy on the island of Reunion. T4: nutmeg and mace come from ONE fruit — nutmeg is the hard SEED, and mace is the red lacy covering (the aril) wrapped around that seed, so a single pit yields two spices. T5 (dinner-test payoff, food-history): that nutmeg fruit grew almost only on the tiny Banda Islands, so the Dutch East India Company massacred and enslaved the islanders in 1621 to seize the monopoly — and in a 1667 treaty the Dutch kept the last nutmeg island (Run) while handing England a swampy island called Manhattan.
source: Verified: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nutmeg (nutmeg=seed, mace=aril of Myristica fragrans; VOC 1621 Banda massacre; 1667 Treaty of Breda Run-for-Manhattan swap), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla (orchid pod, only orchid for food, Mexican, hand-pollination by Edmond Albius 1841 Reunion). Peppercorn=dried fruit, cinnamon=inner bark: settled. Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403).
framing_note: Invert the wonder throughout (superlative/scene in the stem, the plant PART is the answer); never 'What is nutmeg?'. Accuracy rails: nutmeg=seed and mace=aril of the SAME fruit; cinnamon=bark; vanilla is Mexican and hand-pollinated (credit Edmond Albius, an enslaved boy, 1841, Reunion). The Banda rung is food-anchored — nutmeg is the subject that drove the war and the Manhattan swap — and is the flagship payoff; keep the massacre matter-of-fact for a kid, not graphic.

name: Flowers on the plate (the buds and blooms we eat)
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: A surprising amount of dinner is unopened FLOWERS — buds caught before they bloom, or a single flower part dried into treasure. T1: broccoli is a head of unopened flower BUDS; forget it in the garden or fridge and the tight green buds yellow and bloom. T2: a globe artichoke is one giant flower bud — you eat the fleshy base of the leaf-like bracts and the 'heart' (the flower base), while the fuzzy 'choke' is the baby flowers that would open purple if left to grow. T3: a caper is a pickled unopened flower BUD of a Mediterranean bush (and the caper berry is that same flower's fruit) — its punch comes from being brined before it could bloom. T4 (dinner-test payoff): a clove — the little brown spice shaped like a nail — is a dried unopened flower bud of an evergreen tree; that 'nail head' is its folded, unbloomed petals. T5 (invert-the-wonder, flagship): saffron, the world's costliest spice by weight, is only the dried red STIGMA (a thread from the female heart of the flower) of a purple crocus — each flower gives just three threads, so it takes roughly 150 flowers for a single gram.
source: Broccoli/cauliflower = unopened flower buds and artichoke/caper/clove = flower buds, saffron = dried stigmas of Crocus sativus (~150 flowers/g, most-expensive-by-weight): settled botany/culinary fact. Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403); corroborate at build via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saffron, /Clove, /Artichoke, /Caper.
framing_note: Invert the wonder — put the superlative/scene in the stem ('the world's most expensive spice, three threads per flower') and make the knowable flower (the crocus) the answer; never 'What is saffron?'. Accuracy rails: clove = flower bud (not a seed or bark); saffron = stigma. Dinner-test payoff = clove-is-a-flower-bud; the saffron rung is the flagship invert. Numbers (150 flowers/gram) are the hook in the stem, never the tested answer.

name: Roots that hoard the winter (taproots and storage roots)
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: Carrots, beets and their kin are swollen ROOTS — underground pantries a plant fills in year one to bankroll flowering in year two — and that sugar-store is exactly what we harvest. T1: a carrot is a single fat taproot; the plant stuffs it with sugar its first year to fuel a flower stalk its second year, and we harvest the pantry before the plant spends it. T2 (color surprise): carrots were originally purple, white and yellow, not orange — the familiar orange carrot rose in the Netherlands only in the 1500s-1600s (the popular story that Dutch growers bred it orange to honor the House of Orange is a charming LEGEND with little evidence). T3: a beet stores sugar so richly that in cooler climates the sugar in your bowl often comes from the sugar-BEET root rather than tropical cane. T4: a radish's bite (like a turnip's and horseradish's) comes from mustard-oil compounds the root makes for defense — the same chemical family that makes mustard and wasabi sharp. T5 (dinner-test payoff): cassava (the root behind tapioca), a staple for hundreds of millions, is a storage root that is POISONOUS raw — it holds cyanide-releasing compounds and must be grated, soaked, or cooked before it is safe to eat.
source: Verified: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrot (taproot; wild/early carrots purple/white/yellow; orange = Netherlands 16-17c; House-of-Orange tribute is unverified oral tradition/legend), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassava (storage root; linamarin/cyanide, must be processed; South American). Beet-sugar and radish mustard-oils: settled. Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403).
framing_note: Scene-first ('dig up a carrot — why did the plant bother making it?'), never 'What is a root?'. Accuracy rails: orange carrot = Dutch 16-17c and the William-of-Orange tribute is LEGEND (label it as such, don't state it as fact); cassava must be processed to be safe and is South American. Keep the cassava-cyanide rung matter-of-fact. Dinner-test payoff = the cassava rung. The radish-bite chemistry can be a distractor; the tested answer stays food-anchored (the root/vegetable).

name: Stalks and shoots (the stems and leaf-stalks we eat)
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: Some vegetables are the plant's plumbing — young stems and leaf-stalks (petioles) we snap and eat before they turn woody. T1: asparagus is a young STEM — a fast-growing shoot; leave a spear uncut and it rockets up into a tall ferny plant, and the scaly tip is its folded baby leaves. T2: celery is not a stem but a leaf-STALK (petiole) — the part that would hold a leaf up to the sun — and those strings are its water-carrying bundles. T3 (dinner-test payoff, honest safety): rhubarb is a leaf-stalk we cook like fruit, but you eat ONLY the reddish stalk — the big leaves are toxic (loaded with oxalic acid), so they are cut off and thrown away. T4: kohlrabi, that alien-looking bulb-on-a-plate, is a swollen STEM of the cabbage family — proof a 'root vegetable' can actually be a stem sitting above the soil.
source: Asparagus = young stem/shoot, celery = petiole, rhubarb = edible petiole with toxic (oxalic-acid) leaves, kohlrabi = swollen stem (B. oleracea, per the verified Brassica article): settled botany/culinary fact. Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403); corroborate at build via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhubarb and /Asparagus.
framing_note: Lead with the plant's behavior/scene ('leave asparagus uncut — what happens?'), never 'What is a petiole?'. Accuracy rail: rhubarb LEAVES are the toxic part, the stalk is the food — keep it matter-of-fact. Dinner-test payoff = the rhubarb rung (eat the stalk, not the leaf). Tested answers stay food-anchored (which part / which vegetable).

name: The onion family: bulbs and tears (alliums)
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: Onions and garlic are BULBS — underground storage buds wrapped in swollen leaves — and their whole personality (the layers, the tears, the sweet-when-cooked magic) comes from sulfur chemistry the plant built to fend off pests. T1: an onion is a BULB — a short squat stem ringed by fat overlapping storage leaves; every ring you slice is one of those leaves, and the papery skin is the outermost, dried one. T2 (dinner-test payoff, mechanism): cutting an onion ruptures its cells and mixes chemicals into a stinging sulfur gas that drifts up and irritates your eyes — chilling the onion or cutting it under water slows the sting. T3: garlic is a bulb split into cloves, and each clove is itself a little storage bud that can grow a whole new plant; garlic's sharp smell only appears once you crush or cut it and release its sulfur compound. T4: cooking transforms the alliums — heat turns those harsh sulfur compounds into sweet ones, which is why raw garlic bites but roasted garlic goes mild, brown and jammy (a cousin of the browning that sweetens fried onions).
source: Onion/garlic = bulbs of concentric swollen leaf bases; lachrymatory sulfur gas released on cutting; garlic's aroma forms only when crushed; sulfur chemistry mellows with heat: settled culinary/food-science fact. Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403); corroborate at build via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onion, /Garlic, /Syn-Propanethial-S-oxide.
framing_note: Lead with the phenomenon ('why does chopping an onion sting your eyes?'), never 'What is a bulb?'. The mechanism answer stays food-level ('a sulfur gas'), NOT the enzyme/compound Latin name (that name is banned as the tested answer; it may be a distractor). Dinner-test payoff = the tears rung. Keep 'each ring is a leaf' as the T1 wonder.

name: The peanut that buries itself (a legume, not a nut)
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: The peanut breaks every 'nut' rule — it is a bean that flowers in the air then plants its own pods underground, and that legume identity rewrote Southern farming. T1: a peanut is not a nut — it is a LEGUME, a member of the bean and pea family, and it grows inside a pod like other beans. T2 (dinner-test payoff, the amazing fact): the peanut flowers ABOVE ground, then a stalk from the spent flower bends down and pushes the developing pod DOWN INTO the soil, where the peanuts ripen underground (a trick called geocarpy). T3: because it is a legume, the peanut plant hosts bacteria that pull nitrogen out of the air and enrich the soil, so planting peanuts helps refill land that other crops drain. T4 (food-history): George Washington Carver urged Southern farmers to rotate soil-exhausting cotton with peanuts to rebuild worn-out land, then promoted dozens of peanut uses so farmers would have a market for the harvest.
source: Verified: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut (legume in Fabaceae, not a true nut; geocarpy via the peg/gynophore burying the pod; nitrogen-fixing; Carver promoted it as a soil-restoring rotation crop after cotton). Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403).
framing_note: Lead with the paradox/scene ('a peanut plant flowers in the air — so where do the peanuts form?'), never 'What is a legume?'. Accuracy rails: peanut = legume (bean family), NOT a botanical nut; Carver promoted it as a rotation crop and popularizer of uses — he did NOT invent peanut butter, don't imply it. Dinner-test payoff = the geocarpy/buries-itself rung. Keep the answer food-anchored (the peanut/pod/soil), not the bare term 'geocarpy'.

name: Leaves on the plate: greens, herbs, and one famous leaf
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: Leaves are the plant's solar panels, and we eat them fresh (greens), dried (herbs) or steeped (tea) — with the very same leaf giving wildly different results depending on how it is treated. T1: lettuce, spinach, kale and cabbage are LEAVES — a plant's sun-catching solar panels — which is why leafy greens are thin, broad and packed with the green pigment that runs photosynthesis. T2: when lettuce 'bolts' (shoots up to flower in summer heat) it turns bitter — the plant is pouring its energy into seeds and floods the leaves with a bitter milky sap, so gardeners harvest before it bolts. T3: herbs are (mostly) the LEAVES of plants — basil, mint, oregano, bay — while spices come from other parts (bark, seeds, buds, roots); that leaf-vs-other-part line is the simple divide between an herb and a spice. T4 (dinner-test payoff): green tea and black tea come from the SAME leaf (one plant, Camellia sinensis) — the difference is technique, as black tea's leaves are bruised and left to oxidize (darken) while green tea's are heated fast to stop that change. T5: greens fade on purpose in the pot — that vivid broccoli or bean green is chlorophyll, which heat and acid dull to drab olive, so a quick blanch-and-cold-plunge is the cook's trick to keep them bright.
source: Leafy greens = leaves; lettuce bolting turns bitter; herb (leaf) vs spice (other parts); green and black tea both from Camellia sinensis differing by oxidation; chlorophyll dulled by heat/acid: settled culinary/botanical fact. Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403); corroborate at build via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea, /Lettuce, /Herb.
framing_note: Scene-first ('why does lettuce turn bitter in high summer?'), never 'What is a leaf?'. Accuracy rail: green and black tea are the SAME plant, differing only in processing (oxidation), not different species. Dinner-test payoff = the same-leaf tea rung. The herb-vs-spice answer stays food-anchored (leaf vs other part). Don't test pigment chemistry names as the answer.

name: Foods that don't grow the way you'd think
strand: What part of the plant we eat
scope: Some everyday fruits hide astonishing origins — a banana 'tree' that is really a giant herb, a pineapple built from dozens of flowers, a fig that is an inside-out bouquet — plus one clone crop that history already wiped out once. T1: a pineapple doesn't grow on a tree — it grows one-per-plant on a low spiky ground plant, and the whole fruit is DOZENS of separate flowers whose little fruits fused together around a central core (a 'multiple fruit'). T2: a banana 'tree' isn't a tree at all — it is the world's largest HERB, its trunk a tight bundle of leaf-stalks (a pseudostem) with no wood in it, and the banana itself is botanically a berry. T3 (dinner-test payoff, food-history): the banana you eat is a seedless CLONE (the Cavendish); its predecessor, the Gros Michel, was the world's export banana until a soil fungus (Panama disease) wiped it out in the mid-1900s — and the same kind of disease now threatens the Cavendish. T4 (invert-the-wonder): a fig isn't a single fruit — it is an inside-out cluster of tiny flowers sealed inside a fleshy pouch, pollinated by a specialized wasp that crawls in through a pinhole at the tip. T5: a date grows in heavy hanging clusters on a desert palm — one of the oldest cultivated fruits — and it dries and sweetens right on the tree, which is why dates keep for months without spoiling.
source: Verified: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pineapple (multiple fruit of coalesced berries on a low terrestrial bromeliad, one per plant, South American), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana (largest herb, pseudostem of leaf sheaths, fruit is a berry, seedless Cavendish clone, Gros Michel wiped out by Panama disease/Fusarium, TR4 now threatens Cavendish), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fig (syconium of enclosed flowers, fig-wasp pollination via the ostiole). Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403).
framing_note: Lead with the 'you'd never guess' scene, never 'What is a banana?'. Accuracy rails: banana plant = giant herb with no wood and the banana = a berry; the commercial banana is a seedless clone; the Gros Michel-to-Cavendish collapse is food-anchored (the crop is the subject, monoculture the lesson). Dinner-test payoff = the banana-clone/Gros-Michel rung. Keep the fig-wasp rung matter-of-fact.
